The Warty crab, Eriphia verrucosa, exhibits a maximum carapace length of 8 centimeters [Li = 8 centimeters], a size reached by only the largest individuals within the Black Sea and Mediterranean populations. Field surveys conducted along rocky intertidal shores consistently show that ovigerous females attain their highest gonadosomatic index values during the month of May. At a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) for these egg-bearing females reached 16% [GSI = 16%] in late spring.

Reproductive output in female Eriphia verrucosa reaches impressive levels under optimal thermal conditions in the Mediterranean Sea. At a stable temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the annual reproductive output is approximately 224,165 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 224,165 eggs per year], a value derived from counts of eggs carried by the largest ovigerous females. This estimate reflects a single annual brood rather than multiple clutches, as the species appears to concentrate its entire annual reproductive effort into one extended period of brooding. The annual fecundity is immense for a crab of this size and is achieved through the production of thousands of tiny eggs that are brooded externally beneath the abdomen until hatching occurs. Such a high fecundity likely offsets significant larval mortality in the planktonic environment, where predation rates and dispersal risks are substantial for the early zoeal stages that emerge upon hatching.

The larval development of Eriphia verrucosa proceeds through a series of planktonic stages prior to metamorphosis into a benthic juvenile. Rearing experiments conducted at a controlled temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] indicate that the time from hatching to the completion of metamorphosis is 17 days since birth . During this brief but critical period, the free-swimming zoea larvae progress through several moults before reaching the megalopa stage, which then undergoes the morphological transformation into a crablet. The relatively short duration of the larval phase at this elevated temperature suggests a rapid developmental trajectory that may be advantageous in warm, productive coastal waters. In contrast, cooler regimes would likely extend this period considerably, potentially increasing exposure to planktonic predators. The timing of metamorphosis is a key life-history transition, as it marks the shift from a pelagic existence to a demersal lifestyle on the rocky substrates that characterize adult habitats.

Following settlement and metamorphosis, immature Eriphia verrucosa enter a period of somatic growth that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity. Growth trajectory data, informed by comparative studies on congeneric species such as Carcinus maenas, indicate that at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time from birth to puberty is 250 days since birth [tp = 250 days since birth]. Individuals reach this developmental milestone after a prolonged juvenile phase characterized by a series of moulting events that progressively increase body size. The adult female wet weight at first reproduction is approximately 300 grams [Wwi = approximately 300 grams], a substantial mass that reflects the accumulation of somatic tissue and the development of a sufficiently spacious cephalothorax to accommodate the egg mass during brooding. Achieving this size requires efficient foraging on molluscs and crustaceans, which form the bulk of the adult diet in the intertidal zone.

The maximum lifespan of Eriphia verrucosa has been estimated through field recapture studies and extrapolations from related brachyuran species. At a mean annual water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum longevity is 2,190 days [am = 2,190 days]. This relatively extended lifespan for a crab of moderate body size is consistent with a life-history strategy that delays reproductive maturity but allows for multiple breeding seasons. The initial wet weight at birth of an individual larva is extraordinarily small, calculated to be 0.000087114 grams [Wwb = 0.000087114 grams] based on an egg diameter of 550 micrometers. This minute starting mass underscores the enormous fecundity needed to offset the immense mortality suffered during the planktonic larval phase, where only a tiny fraction of the 224,165 eggs produced annually will survive to recruitment into the benthic population.
